episode.observableAction: On a humid Saturday morning in the apartment, the caregiver stands at the small kitchen counter rinsing leafy greens in a plastic basin. The subject sits on the tiled floor nearby with a scattering of plastic animal toys, while the younger sibling watches from a low stool. The caregiver looks over and says in Vietnamese, in a normal speaking voice, for the subject to help by picking up the toys and putting them into a blue basket so the floor can be swept. The caregiver points at the toys and then at the basket beside the fridge. The subject gets up, walks over, and begins gathering the animals one by one, carrying them to the basket and dropping them in. A few pieces roll under the table; the subject crouches, reaches underneath, and pulls them out, adding them to the basket. The younger sibling leans down to hand the subject one toy that was near the stool. When the floor area is mostly clear, the subject nudges the basket closer to the wall with a foot and steps back. The caregiver glances over, sees the cleared space, and moves a broom into position to start sweeping around where the toys had been.

Late on a warm morning in the apartment, the subject and younger sibling sit on the tile floor near a low plastic table with a single red toy truck between them, both pulling on it and trying to direct it in different ways until the caregiver steps from the kitchen, tells them in Vietnamese to stop pulling and take turns, after which the subject releases the truck and watches while the younger sibling hugs it, then sets it down and pushes it in a circle on the floor.

On a late morning in the apartment, the caregiver stands near the doorway holding a small bunch of keys and a cloth shopping bag, calling out in Vietnamese that they are getting ready to go to the market. The subject looks around the living room, then walks to the low table where a plastic pencil case usually sits and finds the spot empty. The subject says that their pencil case is missing and starts checking under a stack of school notebooks, then lifts a thin cushion from the floor and looks underneath. The younger sibling, sitting on the tiled floor with a toy, watches and then points toward the sofa. The subject kneels by the sofa, reaches a hand between the seat cushion and the armrest, and pulls out the blue plastic pencil case, which has slid partly open with a pencil sticking out. The subject snaps it shut, stands up, and carries it over to their school bag hanging on a hook by the door, unzips the bag, and places the case inside. The caregiver glances over, sees the subject zipping the bag, and says in Vietnamese that now they can go, then turns the doorknob while the subject steps into sandals by the threshold.

At a neighborhood market on a warm Sunday morning, the caregiver and a nearby adult relative stand with the subject near a vegetable stall as the caregiver, holding a cloth shopping bag and a folded list, tells the subject in Vietnamese to go alone to the next row to buy half a kilo of tomatoes, to check the price, and not to forget the change, then presses a 20,000 đồng note into the subject’s hand and points toward stalls around the corner; the subject walks alone along the crowded aisle past greens and chilies to a stall with a low table of red tomatoes, asks the shopkeeper in a conical hat for half a kilo, holds out the money, waits while she weighs and bags the tomatoes, then receives coins and a smaller note as change, glances at it, and walks back through the same aisle to the caregiver and relative, where the subject hands over the bag of tomatoes and shows the remaining money as the caregiver nods and slips the tomatoes into the larger cloth bag while the relative watches.

On a humid mid-morning in the apartment, the caregiver stands near the doorway holding a motorbike helmet and a small cloth bag, calling out in Vietnamese that they need to leave soon for an errand and asking the younger sibling which sandals to wear, pointing toward a pair of faded blue sandals and a newer red pair lined up by the wall. The younger sibling hesitates, looking back and forth between them. The subject, already wearing school shorts and a T-shirt, walks over from the low table, crouches beside the sandals, and picks up one blue and one red sandal, holding them side by side so the younger sibling can see the difference in size and wear. The subject says in Vietnamese that the blue pair is more comfortable for walking far but the red pair looks nicer, then sets both pairs down neatly in front of the younger sibling. The younger sibling studies them for a moment, then reaches out and chooses the red pair, slipping their feet into them. The subject steps back to give space while the caregiver glances over, sees the choice, and says in Vietnamese that the red sandals are fine, before turning toward the door to unlock it.

In the apartment, the caregiver shows limited cash and a nearly empty dish soap bottle, asks the subject to choose between buying snacks or soap, and the subject inspects the bottle, explains in Vietnamese that soap is needed to wash dishes, persuades the younger sibling by comparing choosing soap now and snacks later, then tells the caregiver to buy dish soap.

At the neighborhood market entrance, the caregiver gives the subject money and a list, tells them in Vietnamese to buy dish soap and rice, waits by a fruit stall while the subject walks through the crowd to two stalls to purchase a medium bottle of dish soap and two kilos of mid-priced rice, pays with the given cash, receives change, then returns and hands the items and remaining money to the caregiver.

On a humid Sunday morning in the apartment, the caregiver places a small stack of cash and a nearly empty bottle of cooking oil on a low plastic table, tells the subject and younger sibling in Vietnamese that there is only enough money to buy either oil or snacks, and steps into the nearby kitchen area to rinse dishes while remaining within earshot as the younger sibling says they want snacks, the subject uses a notebook and pen to write and say that oil is for cooking meals and snacks are just for today, shows the thin layer of oil left in the bottle, sketches a pan with an egg to illustrate having fried eggs with rice after school, and then leaves the decision to the sibling, who looks between the oil and the cash and states in Vietnamese that they choose oil, after which the subject repeats this choice toward the kitchen and the caregiver returns to confirm they will buy cooking oil and picks up the cash and bottle while the children stay seated on the floor.

On a warm Saturday morning in the apartment, the caregiver places a small stack of cash, a nearly empty bag of rice, and a snack flyer on the low plastic table, explains in Vietnamese that there is only enough money either for a full sack of rice or for a smaller amount of rice plus some snacks, and asks the subject and younger sibling to decide while they wash clothes on the balcony; after the caregiver steps outside, the younger sibling points at chips and sweet drinks on the flyer, the subject shakes the thin rice bag to show how little is left, writes two short columns on scrap paper labeled “chỉ gạo” and “gạo + bánh” with the prices for a full sack versus a smaller bag plus two snacks, points to the circled full-sack price while saying the smaller bag might run out before the end of the week, and after the sibling hesitates and then agrees to choose the full sack of rice, the subject calls this choice toward the balcony, shows the paper when the caregiver returns, and the caregiver nods, takes the cash and old rice bag, leaves the folded flyer on the table, and says they will go to the market for rice while the siblings stay in the apartment.

On a warm Sunday morning in the apartment, the caregiver sits at a low plastic table with a folded notice from the neighborhood public school and a small notebook, calls the subject and younger sibling over, and explains in Vietnamese that the school is offering an optional extra English class after regular hours for a monthly fee, shows that paying for it would mean not affording the younger sibling’s planned weekend drawing course, and after the subject reads the notice, asks questions, and looks at the sibling, the subject tells the caregiver to register them for the extra English class instead of the drawing course, and the caregiver fills out and tears off the registration slip while the younger sibling remains seated and silent.

The subject kneels by the sofa, reaches a hand between the seat cushion and the armrest, and pulls out the blue plastic pencil case, which has slid partly open with a pencil sticking out. The subject snaps it shut, stands up, and carries it over to their school bag hanging on a hook by the door, unzips the bag, and places the case inside. The caregiver glances over, sees the subject zipping the bag, and says in Vietnamese that now they can go, then turns the doorknob while the subject steps into sandals by the threshold.
